newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Main parties, leaders in Algeria's new parliament.
newsitem.headline: Main parties, leaders in Algeria's new parliament.

text.p: Six parties dominate Algeria's new parliament, lead by a strong backer of President Liamine Zeroual, official results of the general election showed on Friday.

The ballot was the first since the nation's experiment with a multi-party general election was cancelled in 1992 after the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) massively led the first round. The FIS needed only 28 more seats for a parliamentary majority.
Years of bloodshed followed the cancellation. The FIS is outlawed and could not stand in Thursday's ballot.
Following are details of the parties and their key people.
NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC RALLY (RND)
155 seats, 3.5 million votes.

The RND, founded in early April, groups Zeroual's core political supporters. Its platform is inspired largely by Zeroual's programme pledging to restore peace and stability, a cautious approach to privatising state-owned companies and a welfare scheme focusing on helping the poor affected by the economy's transition towards a free market.

Algerian critics say the newly created RND showed the government's eagerness to firm up its own political base in the new parliament. The aim, they say, is to use the "democratic weapon" to marginalise main legal opposition groups.
RND leaders say the party was created to fill a political void left by fractious opposition leaders who failed to answer mainstream Algerian needs.

The RND is headed by Abdelkader Bensalah, president of government-appointed Transitional National Council, a quasi-parliament. Bensalah, 56, was a Foreign Ministry spokesman in 1992 and is a former parliament deputy.
MOVEMENT OF A PEACEFUL SOCIETY (MPS)
69 seats, 1.5 million votes

Algeria's main legal Islamist party changed its name early in April to conform to a new law banning political parties based on Islam. The former Movement of the Islamic Society -- known by its Arabic acronym Hamas -- became Movement of a Peaceful Society.
But the name change did not alter the group's core policies.

It is led by Mahfoud Nahnah, a telegenic and colourful former Arabic language teacher and imam. He has transformed from a radical Molsem fundamentalist firebrand in the 1980s into an "objective ally" of a government engaged in a merciless battle against the radical Islamists.
Critics say Nahnah is engaged in "back-scratching" with the military which is trying to wipe out his bitter rivals in the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).
The party officially advocates "incremental change" through dialogue and participation in political life. It joined in Zeroual's government in 1995 taking two junior portfolios.

It advocates a leading role for the private sector in the economy, and focuses on promises to ease the plight of the jobless -- 2.5 million mainly young unemployed. It also says government must finance the construction of small homes to help young people get married. Thousands of young Algerians are unable to marry because of the chronic housing shortage.
Nahnah took one-third of a 1995 presidential vote won by Zeroual.
NATIONAL LIBERATION FRONT (FLN)
64 seats, 1.4 million votes

The FLN is the founder of the Algerian nation, having led seven years of bloody war to end more than a century of French colonial rule in 1962. The party ruled Algeria until its grip on power was loosened by growing opposition and the dwindling value of oil and gas exports in the late 1980s.

It was humiliated in two successive elections in 1990 and 1991 at the hands of emerging radical Islamists. FLN joined the opposition camp early in 1992, attacking the authorities for scrapping a general poll in which Islamists were leading.
The party changed its leadership in 1995 and altered its policy hoping to get closer to Zeroual, but the move backfired after the president's supporters created RND.
Headed by former finance minister Boualem Benhamouda, it promises stability and peace.
NAHDA MOVEMENT
34 seats, 0.9 million votes.

Another moderate Islamist movement which in February changed its name from the former Nahda Islamic Movement in order to conform to the new law. Headed by Abdallah Djaballah who says he was involved in mediation efforts between Zeroual and jailed FIS leaders Abassi Madani and Ali Belhadj before these collapsed with Zeroual accusing the FIS of intransigence.
SOCIALIST FORCES FRONT (FFS)
19 seats, 0.4 million votes.

FFS was created in 1963 in opposition to then president Ahmed Ben Bella's one-party rule. It draws its main support from the northeastern areas dominated by Algerian Berbers and middle-class urban residents in Algiers and some other cities.

It insists that dialogue with the main opposition, including the FIS, is the only way out of Algeria's crisis. It advocates a moderate role for the government in the economy and a more even distribution of the nation's income.
RALLY FOR DEMOCRACY AND CULTURE (RCD)
19 seats, 0.4 million votes.
The RCD was set up in 1989 by former FFS members. It is the staunchest backer of the military against Moslem rebels.

Its leader, Said Saadi, 50, won 10 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll. The RCD advocates a Turkish-style secular state, saying the politicisation of the Moslem faith has caused havoc in Algeria.
